subject: Career
title: Negotiating a Raise vs. a New Offer
description: A quick win: understand Negotiating a Raise vs. a New Offer.

hook.text: Asking your current boss for a raise feels scarier than negotiating with a stranger. Here's why.

buildup.text: With a new offer, you have leverage: they need you. With a raise, you're renegotiating existing terms.

discovery.text: For raises, build a case over months: document impact, collect praise, track market data.

twist.text: Timing matters enormously. Ask after a big win, during budget season, never during layoffs.

climax.text: Frame it as alignment: 'My role has grown. I'd like my compensation to reflect that.'

punchline.text: Raises aren't given. They're built and then requested.

quiz.question: When is the best time to ask for a raise?
options: After a big win during budget season

details.summary: Negotiating a raise internally and negotiating a new offer externally involve different power dynamics, risk profiles, and strategies. Internal raises leverage loyalty and institutional knowledge, while external offers leverage market competition and fresh starts.
details.whyItMatters: Choosing the wrong strategy can stall your career or burn bridges. Understanding when an internal raise outperforms a job switch, and vice versa, optimizes long-term earnings.
takeaways: Internal raises preserve equity vesting and institutional capital
External moves often yield larger single-step salary increases
Calculate the total switching cost before accepting a new offer

faq.question: When is an external offer clearly the better financial move?
faq.answer: When the internal pay gap exceeds fifteen to twenty percent and your employer has shown no willingness to close it, an external move is typically rational. Also consider whether the new role offers growth opportunities your current position cannot match.

faq.question: Can I use an external offer to negotiate an internal raise?
faq.answer: Yes, but use this tactic sparingly. Presenting an external offer as a retention case works once. Repeated use erodes trust and signals to management that you are perpetually flight-risk, which can limit future opportunities.
